title: File Upload API Design
description: Design a file upload API supporting chunked uploads, resumable transfers, virus scanning, and metadata extraction for large files.

data.text: File upload APIs must handle large files, unreliable networks, and security scanning. Simple multipart form uploads fail for files over 100MB. You need chunked uploads, resumable transfers, and a clear lifecycle from upload initiation to final storage.

items: Initiate — client requests an upload URL and receives an upload ID
Upload chunks — client sends file parts (5-10MB each)
Verify — client asks the server to verify all chunks arrived
Complete — server assembles chunks, runs virus scan, and stores the final file

data.title: Resumable upload flow using TUS-style chunked uploads
data.content: TUS is an open protocol for resumable uploads. The client requests an upload, sends chunks, and can resume after network failures.
data.code:
# Step 1: Initiate upload
POST /uploads
Upload-Length: 104857600
Upload-Metadata: filename dGVzdC5tcDM=

Response: 201 Created
Location: /uploads/upload_991
Upload-Expires: 2026-10-06T16:00:00Z

# Step 2: Upload chunk 1 (5MB)
PATCH /uploads/upload_991
Content-Type: application/offset+octet-stream
Upload-Offset: 0
[binary chunk data]

Response: 204 No Content
Upload-Offset: 5242880

# Step 3: Upload chunk 2
PATCH /uploads/upload_991
Content-Type: application/offset+octet-stream
Upload-Offset: 5242880
[binary chunk data]

Response: 204 No Content
Upload-Offset: 10485760

items: Scan every chunk as it arrives; do not wait for assembly
Enforce file size limits per user tier (free: 100MB, pro: 10GB)
Validate content type server-side; never trust client-provided MIME types
Store files outside the web root with signed, time-limited download URLs
Use CORS to restrict upload origins to your frontend domain

data.title: Virus scanning is mandatory
data.text: Never expose uploaded files to other users without scanning. Integrate ClamAV or a cloud-based malware scanner in the chunk processing pipeline. A single malicious file can compromise your entire infrastructure.

data.title: POST /uploads/{id}/complete — Finalize upload
data.content: After all chunks are uploaded, the client requests completion. The server assembles the file, runs virus scan, extracts metadata, and returns the canonical file resource.

items.question: Should I upload directly to S3 or through my API server?
items.answer: For files over 10MB, use pre-signed S3 URLs. Your API generates the upload URL and validates the final file. This keeps your API servers fast and avoids scaling bottlenecks.

items.question: What chunk size should I use?
items.answer: 5-10MB chunks balance retry cost and overhead. Smaller chunks reduce wasted uploads on failure but increase the number of requests. Larger chunks reduce overhead but waste more on retry.

items.question: How do I handle upload resumption after a network drop?
items.answer: The client stores the upload ID and last successful offset. On reconnect, it sends PATCH with Upload-Offset set to the last received value. The server appends from that point.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Large files need chunked, resumable uploads, not single-shot multipart.
Scan chunks as they arrive; never trust client content types.
Use pre-signed storage URLs for files over 10MB.
Upload IDs must be non-guessable to prevent enumeration.
data.takeaway: A production upload API treats large files as a streaming problem, not a request body problem. Chunk, scan, and store outside the web root.
